questions.q: How do you install the ZudoJS command-line tool, and what is the command called?
questions.explain: The CLI is published as zudojs-cli and gives you the zudojs command. There is no npm package called zudo or zudojs, and every framework package is named @zudojs/something.
options: npm install -g zudojs, and the command is zudo
npm install -g zudojs-cli, and the command is zudojs
npm install -g @zudojs/cli, and the command is zudojs-cli
npm install zudo, and the command is npx zudo

questions.q: What does the -g in npm install -g zudojs-cli do?
questions.explain: A global install puts the zudojs command on your whole computer. -D, not -g, is the flag for a dev dependency.
options: It installs the package as a dev dependency of the current project
It installs a smaller "general" version of the package
It installs the package globally, so the command works in any folder
It skips the download and uses a cached copy

questions.q: On Linux, npm install -g zudojs-cli fails with a permission error (EACCES). What does the lesson recommend?
questions.explain: Don't fix it with sudo: that runs a package's install scripts with full system rights. npx zudojs-cli --version and npx zudojs-cli create … work for every command without a global install.
options: Run it again with sudo in front
Change the owner of every system folder to your user
Skip the global install and use npx zudojs-cli … instead
Install an older version of Node.js

questions.q: Why does the lesson pass --package-manager npm?
questions.explain: The CLI supports pnpm, npm, Yarn and Bun, and defaults to pnpm. The course uses npm because it comes with Node.js.
options: Because ZudoJS projects only work with npm
The CLI's default is pnpm, which you would have to install first; npm you already have
Because npm is the only manager that can install @zudojs packages
Because pnpm cannot run the dev script

questions.q: What does --capabilities "" mean when you create the project?
questions.explain: Capabilities such as Queue or Observability are optional. Starting with none keeps the project small; zudojs add brings each one in when the course needs it.
options: Add every optional capability at once
Ask about the capabilities later, when the server starts
Start with no optional extras; add them one at a time later with zudojs add
Create a project without any @zudojs packages at all

questions.q: What happens if you run zudojs create with no name and no options?
questions.explain: Every flag answers one of the questions (name, type, architecture, database, API style, package manager, capabilities). Leave a flag out and the CLI asks.
options: It fails with "missing project name"
It creates a project called my-project without asking
It becomes interactive and asks one question at a time; the flags just answer them in advance
It prints the help text and exits

questions.q: After create, npm reports some moderate vulnerabilities, all in Vitest, the test runner. What is the right reaction?
questions.explain: Read the report first. Here the issues are in a tool that runs only on your own computer, and --force would jump Vitest two major versions. In packages that run in production, you would take them seriously.
options: Run npm audit fix --force at once
Delete the tests folder so Vitest is not needed
Run npm audit to read them; they are in a dev-only tool, and --force would make breaking upgrades
Ignore every npm audit message from now on

questions.q: npm run dev runs tsx watch src/server.ts. What does watch add?
questions.explain: tsx runs TypeScript directly, and watch restarts it on every save. That is why a change to the health controller shows up without restarting by hand.
options: It prints every request the server receives
It restarts the server every time you save a file
It compiles the project into the dist folder
It checks the types before each request

questions.q: The server says Listening on port 3000, and you open http://localhost:3000/health. What do localhost and 3000 mean?
questions.explain: Each program that listens for network requests uses its own port. localhost:3000 reaches the program on your own computer listening on port 3000.
options: localhost is the ZudoJS website; 3000 is your user number
localhost means "this computer"; 3000 is the numbered door the server listens on
localhost is your router; 3000 is the number of allowed requests
localhost is a test database; 3000 is its size in megabytes

questions.q: Why does GET /tasks answer 404 in the new project?
questions.explain: A new project has a health check but no task routes. A path with no route gets a 404 with a JSON body, the same status-plus-body pattern as in Your first Zudo code.
options: Because the server is not running yet
Because you are not logged in
Because no route serves /tasks yet; building it is the next part of the course
Because /tasks is blocked in development mode

questions.q: What is .env.example for?
questions.explain: It shows which settings exist. Real passwords and keys go only into the real environment, never into files you share or commit.
options: It holds the real production passwords, so the team can share them
It lists the settings the app reads from the environment, such as PORT, without real secrets
It is loaded instead of package.json in production
It is a test file that Vitest runs

questions.q: What is .zudojs/manifest.json for?
questions.explain: The CLI reads it to learn, for example, that the project is a monolith, and chooses folders to match. Don't edit it by hand.
options: It is the list of npm packages; npm reads it on install
It records what the CLI knows about the project, so commands like generate put files in the right place
It stores the logs of the running server
It holds your TypeScript settings

questions.q: The generated app builds a runtime. What is its job?
questions.explain: This is the lifecycle job from What a framework does: start in dependency order, stop in reverse. Modules are the pieces it starts and stops.
options: It compiles TypeScript to JavaScript
It answers the /health request
It starts and stops every piece of the app in the right order
It installs the project's npm packages

questions.q: You run npm run typecheck (tsc --noEmit) and it prints nothing after the script line. What does that mean?
questions.explain: --noEmit checks the types without writing files, and silence means success. Tests are a separate script: npm test.
options: The check did not run
There are no type errors
The compiled files were written to dist
The tests passed

questions.q: Something seems wrong with your setup. Which command should you run first?
questions.explain: doctor checks Node.js, the package manager, dependencies and the project files, and tells you what is wrong. info only shows versions and packages.
options: zudojs info
zudojs build
zudojs doctor
npm audit fix --force

questions.q: What does zudojs generate service task --dry-run do?
questions.explain: --dry-run is a safe way to learn where each kind of file belongs. Without it, generate writes the files and adds the exports.
options: It writes the files and runs their tests
It lists the files it would write, and writes nothing
It writes the files but does not add them to index.ts
It deletes any existing service called task

questions.q: What does zudojs add database do?
questions.explain: add installs a feature's package. Writing the database code is still your job, with the package's help.
options: It creates the database tables for your tasks
It writes a TaskRepository with SQL for you
It adds the @zudojs/database package to the project and records the feature
It starts a PostgreSQL server on your computer

questions.q: What should you do right after zudojs generate writes new files?
questions.explain: Templates cannot know everything about your project. The type check tells you at once whether the new files fit; fix what tsc reports.
options: Nothing: generated files are always final
Delete .zudojs/manifest.json so the CLI forgets them
Run npm run typecheck, because generated files are a starting point
Run npm audit fix --force

questions.q: Why do you build for production instead of running npm run dev on the server?
questions.explain: npm run build runs tsc, which writes a JavaScript twin of each src/ file into dist/. npm start then runs node dist/server.js: no tsx, no watching.
options: Because tsx cannot run on Linux servers
A production server should not compile TypeScript on the fly or watch files; compile once and run plain JavaScript
Because the build removes all the @zudojs packages
Because npm run dev does not listen on a port

questions.q: You change the health controller, then run npm start. The old answer comes back. Why?
questions.explain: start runs dist/server.js, not your TypeScript. Rebuild after every change, or use npm run dev while developing.
options: The browser cached the page; press reload
Port 3000 is still used by the old server
npm start runs the compiled dist/ files, built before your change; run npm run build again
The change only takes effect after zudojs doctor

questions.q: A hosting platform sends SIGTERM when it replaces your app. What does a graceful shutdown do?
questions.explain: The server stops first, then the runtime stops each module in reverse, so nothing is cut off halfway. The time limit (30 s here) stops a hanging module from blocking forever.
options: It kills the process at once, so the new version starts faster
It keeps the old app running forever next to the new one
It stops taking new requests, then stops every module in reverse order, with a time limit
It restarts the app with the same code

questions.q: Why does the generated .gitignore list dist/?
questions.explain: Anyone can recreate dist/ with npm run build. Committing it would only create noise and stale copies. The deployment lesson builds it inside a Docker image.
options: Because dist/ contains your passwords
Build output is made from the source, so it never belongs in git
Because git cannot store JavaScript files
Because dist/ is deleted on every npm run dev

questions.q: The generated health check answers 200 only while the runtime is running. What does this print?
questions.explain: 503 Service Unavailable tells a load balancer "don't send me traffic yet" while the app starts, and again while it shuts down. Only a running app says 200.
options:
starting 200
running 200
stopping 200

starting 503
running 200
stopping 503

starting 503
running 200
stopping 200

starting 404
running 200
stopping 404

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Paths are compared exactly, so /Health with a capital H is a different path. Every miss still gets a status and a JSON body.

questions.q: curl -i showed content-length: 54 for the health answer. What does this print?
questions.explain: The response body is JSON text, and content-length is its size: here 54 characters (bytes, since it is all plain ASCII). .length of an object would be undefined; of the string it is 54.
options:
{"status":"ok","timestamp":"2026-09-23T12:22:38.526Z"}
undefined

questions.q: The health controller returns new Date().toISOString(). What does this fixed-date version print?
questions.explain: Months in Date.UTC start at 0, so 8 is September. toISOString() always gives this standard UTC format ending in Z, which is why the timestamps in the logs look alike on every computer.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The host is localhost (this computer), the port is 3000 (the server's door), and the path /health is what the server's handler compares.
questions.code:
const url = new URL("http://localhost:3000/health");
console.log(url.hostname, url.port, url.pathname);
options: localhost:3000 3000 health
localhost 3000 /health
localhost 3000 health
http://localhost 3000 /health

questions.q: The server reads its port from a setting. What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing PORT falls back to 3000. Environment values are always text, so Number converts "4000". "http" becomes NaN, which is not an integer, so the app refuses to start.
options:
3000
"4000"
Invalid PORT: http

3000
4000
Invalid PORT: http

undefined
4000
Invalid PORT: http

questions.q: With "rootDir": "src" and "outDir": "dist", tsc writes a JavaScript twin of each file. What does this sketch print?
questions.explain: The folder structure is kept, src/ becomes dist/, and .ts becomes .js. That is why the start script is node dist/server.js.
options:
dist/server.ts
dist/controllers/health.controller.ts

src/server.js
src/controllers/health.controller.js

dist/server.js
dist/controllers/health.controller.js

dist/server.js
dist/health.controller.js

questions.q: A sketch of "change the code, but forget to rebuild". What does it print?
questions.explain: The build copies the code as it was at that moment. npm start runs that copy, so your change appears only after you build again.
options:
npm start: {"status":"ok","service":"task-api"}
after build: {"status":"ok","service":"task-api"}

npm start: {"status":"ok"}
after build: {"status":"ok","service":"task-api"}

npm start: {"status":"ok"}
after build: {"status":"ok"}

npm start: undefined
after build: {"status":"ok","service":"task-api"}

questions.q: A sketch of generate with and without --dry-run. What does it print?
questions.explain: A dry run still works out the list of files (2), but writes none of them. Only the real run adds them.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: NODE_ENV=production is the usual way to tell a Node.js app it runs in production. Environment variables are strings in process.env, and code can read them to decide how to behave.
options: development true
production true
production false
undefined false

questions.q: What does this print? (process.emit calls the listeners, as if the signal arrived.)
questions.explain: process.once only registers the handler; it runs when SIGTERM arrives. The server stops taking requests first, then the parts stop in reverse start order (http started last, so it stops first).
options:
stop taking requests
stopped: http, orders, database
Listening on port 3000

Listening on port 3000
stop taking requests
stopped: http, orders, database
Listening on port 3000

Listening on port 3000
stopped: database, orders, http

questions.q: A shutdown with a time limit. What does this print?
questions.explain: A module that stops in time wins the race. One that never finishes would block shutdown forever, so the limit ends the wait. The generated app uses 30 seconds.
options:
stopped
stopped

stopped
timed out

timed out
timed out
stopped

questions.q: Finish check(runtimeState). While the runtime is "running", return { status: 200, body: { status: "ok" } }. In any other state, return { status: 503, body: { status: "unavailable" } }.
questions.explain: Check for the one good state and treat everything else as unavailable. A 503 tells load balancers not to send traffic to an app that is starting or stopping.

questions.q: Finish the HealthController from the practice exercise: check(now) returns { status: "ok", service: "task-api", timestamp }, where timestamp is now as an ISO string. (The date is passed in so the output is always the same.)
questions.explain: A controller is an ordinary class that returns the response body. toISOString() gives the standard UTC format that clients can parse anywhere.

questions.q: Finish handler(request, runtimeState): for path /health, answer 200 { status: "ok" } when the runtime is running, else 503 { status: "unavailable" }. Every other path gets 404 { error: "Not Found" }.
questions.explain: Every request reaches the handler, and every answer is a status plus a JSON body. The next part of the course replaces this if with a real router.

questions.q: Finish resolvePort(env): use env.PORT, or 3000 when it is missing. It must be a whole number from 1 to 65535; otherwise throw an Error with the message Invalid PORT.
questions.explain: Environment values are text, so convert with Number, then check. A bad port should stop the app at startup, not fail later in a confusing way.
questions.expected:
3000 8080
abc Invalid PORT
0 Invalid PORT
70000 Invalid PORT
80.5 Invalid PORT

questions.q: Finish outputFor(sourcePath): with rootDir src and outDir dist, turn a source path into the path of its compiled twin.
questions.explain: Swap the src/ prefix for dist/ and the .ts ending for .js; the folders in between stay the same. replace with /^src\// and /\.ts$/ works too.

questions.q: Finish shutdown(server, modules): first stop the server (await server.stop()), then stop the modules in reverse order, then print shutdown complete. Do not change the modules array.
questions.explain: Stop taking requests first, then close each part while the parts it needs still run. Copy the array with [...modules] before reverse(), which would otherwise change it.
questions.expected:
server stopped
app stopped
database stopped
config stopped
shutdown complete
config,database,app

questions.q: Finish generate(schematic, name, options). For "service" the files are src/services/NAME/NAME.service.ts and src/services/NAME/index.ts; for "repository" they are src/repositories/NAME.repository.ts and src/repositories/index.ts. Add them to written only when options.dryRun is not true. Always return the list.
questions.explain: Work out the file list first, then decide whether to write. That is what --dry-run does: the same plan, with nothing written.
